text: Look at these hills. They look as if a giant dropped millions of boulders and walked away. Nobody dropped them. Every one of these rocks was shaped underground, inside granite roughly two and a half billion years old. And around the year fifteen hundred, the city built among them is estimated to have been the second largest city in the world, after Beijing. This is Hampi, in Karnataka. In the next few minutes: how the boulders really formed, how an empire built a capital out of them, how it fell in six months, and what archaeologists have dug up here this November.
Hampi. Why it's covered in giant boulders.

Hampi sits on the banks of the Tungabhadra river, in the eastern part of central Karnataka. The nearest big town is Hosapete, about thirteen kilometres away, and Bengaluru is roughly three hundred and forty kilometres to the south. From the air, the land around it looks almost unreal: ridge after ridge of golden granite, piled into heaps, with the river cutting straight through.

Local legend has a simple explanation. In the Ramayana, this is Kishkindha, the kingdom of the monkey brothers Vali and Sugreeva. One story says the boulders were hurled during their great fight. Another says they were piled up to build the bridge to Lanka. Sugreeva is said to have hidden on Matanga Hill, the tallest hill in Hampi, because a curse stopped Vali from climbing it. It's a great story. The geology is just as dramatic.

Start with the rock itself. Hampi stands on the Dharwar craton, one of the oldest, most stable pieces of India's crust. The granite here began as molten magma that pushed into the crust deep underground, in the Late Archaean, roughly two and a half billion years ago. It cooled very slowly, miles below the surface. And as it cooled, it shrank and cracked into a grid of horizontal and vertical fractures. Geologists call them joints. Those cracks decided the shape of every boulder you see today.

Here's the key step, and it happened below ground. Rainwater seeps down through the joints. It reacts with the feldspar in the granite and slowly turns the rock along the cracks into soft clay and crumbly grit, called grus. The corners of each block are attacked from two or three sides at once, so they rot away fastest. Edges round off. Square blocks become rounded cores of hard, fresh rock, wrapped in rotten rock. Geologists call these corestones.

Then the land above wears away. Rain, gravity and wind carry the loose grus off, and the hard corestones are left behind, stacked more or less where they formed. That's why so many Hampi boulders sit on top of each other, some balanced on surprisingly small points of contact. Hills like these have names: tors, and the bigger ones inselbergs, from the German for island mountain. How long all of this took is still debated, but every estimate is vast compared with human history.

Let's put that at true scale. Squeeze the granite's two and a half billion years into a single day. The Vijayanagara empire ruled from Hampi for two hundred and twenty nine years, from thirteen thirty six to fifteen sixty five. On that clock, its whole reign lasts less than one hundredth of a second. The rocks were ancient long before anyone arrived. But for those two centuries, this landscape held one of the great cities on Earth.

In thirteen thirty six, two brothers, Harihara the First and Bukka the First, founded the Vijayanagara empire, and Hampi became its capital. It sat beside the river, in hilly terrain made of granite boulders. The empire grew rich, and India's Ministry of Culture notes it was enriched by the cotton and spice trade. For more than two centuries, this was the heart of a powerful South Indian kingdom.

How big did it get? Historians such as Nicholas Gier estimate that by fifteen hundred it was the world's second largest city, after Beijing, and probably India's richest. Visitors were stunned. Abdur Razzaq, a Persian envoy, came to the court of Devaraya the Second. The Italian Niccolo de Conti came too. And around fifteen twenty, the Portuguese traveller Domingo Paes visited under Krishnadevaraya and compared the size of the city to Rome.

And much of it was carved from granite. The Virupaksha temple has a gateway tower about fifty metres high, and parts of the temple complex existed by the eleventh century. Worship there has never stopped. At the Vittala temple stands the stone chariot, a shrine to Garuda carved in the form of a chariot, the image you'll find on India's fifty rupee note. Inside, a hall of carved granite pillars makes musical sounds when they're struck.

Then, in fifteen sixty five, it ended. At the Battle of Talikota, an alliance of Deccan sultanates defeated the Vijayanagara army and captured and beheaded its leader, Aliya Rama Raya. The capital was pillaged, looted and burnt for six months, then abandoned. Two centuries of building, wrecked in half a year. In eighteen hundred, Colin Mackenzie surveyed the ruins, and in nineteen hundred Robert Sewell called it a forgotten empire.

In nineteen eighty six, UNESCO listed the Group of Monuments at Hampi as a World Heritage Site. From nineteen ninety nine to two thousand and six, it was on the list of sites in danger. The protected area covers about four thousand one hundred and eighty seven hectares, roughly forty two square kilometres, and UNESCO counts more than sixteen hundred surviving remains. Temples, palaces, markets, water tanks and gateways, scattered through the boulders.

And Hampi is still giving up secrets. In May twenty twenty six, the Archaeological Survey of India found a buried stone ceiling and rare elephant carvings near the Hazara Rama temple, part of a structure about four point three by four point two metres. Then, on the fourteenth of November, it reported the remains of two more temples, one to Vishnu and one to Shiva, near the Ganagitti temple, Hampi's oldest Jain shrine, dated to thirteen eighty six.

So why go now? Because this is the season. Karnataka Tourism recommends October to February, and suggests about three days to see it properly. Take the train to Hosapete Junction, about thirteen kilometres away. Climb Matanga Hill, the highest viewpoint in central Hampi, for sunset over the boulders. Take a coracle, a round traditional boat, on the Tungabhadra. And if your dates allow it, catch the Hampi festival, when music and dance return to the ruins.

One honest note before you go. These ruins are fragile, and they have survived more than four and a half centuries since the city was abandoned. Don't climb on carved monuments, and remember that Virupaksha is a living temple, not just a ruin. The boulders will outlast all of us. The carvings might not.

So, two and a half billion years to make the boulders, two centuries to build a great city among them, and six months to destroy it. Now tell me in the comments: the legend of Vali and Sugreeva, or the geology, which story do you find more amazing? And if you like seeing places at their true scale, subscribe to True Scale.
